text: In the terraced city of Solgrove, a lumenwright is an artisan who cultivates living crystals of light called lumens. The craft is older than the city walls, and its practitioners guard their methods within the Verdant Accord.

A lumen begins as a sablecore, a dull grey seed no larger than a thumbnail. When a sablecore is bathed in dawnglass dust and kept in resonance, it slowly brightens until it hums with a soft inner glow.

Dawnglass is a powdered mineral harvested from the cliffs east of Solgrove. Lumenwrights prize the palest dawnglass, which they call first-light grade, because it coaxes the steadiest glow from a young sablecore.

Resonance-tuning is the heart of lumenwrighting. By striking tuned rods called caril forks, a lumenwright sets the air around a sablecore vibrating at the pitch the crystal prefers. A well-tuned room is said to be in accord.
Every lumen has a preferred pitch known as its keynote. Apprentices spend their first year learning to hear keynotes by ear, a skill the masters call listening true.
The Verdant Accord is the guild that governs lumenwrights. It was founded after the Dimming, a year when every lumen in Solgrove went dark at once and the city nearly froze in the long night.

A lumen that loses its glow is called a guttered crystal. Skilled lumenwrights can sometimes rekindle a guttered crystal through patient resonance-tuning, but a crystal that stays dark for a full season is considered spent.

Lumens are sorted by brightness into three grades. A hearthlumen gives gentle warmth and light for a single room. A wardlumen can light a courtyard. A beaconlumen, rarest of all, can crown a tower and be seen across the valley.

The cultivation of a beaconlumen may take a lumenwright twenty years. Such a crystal is never sold; it is entrusted, and the lumenwright who raised it is bound to tend it until death by the oaths of the Verdant Accord.
Solgrove measures its wealth not in coin but in candlemarks, the standard unit of stored lumen-light. A single hearthlumen yields roughly four hundred candlemarks before it must rest and be re-tuned.
Lumenwrights speak of a crystal resting when its glow dims naturally after long use. A rested lumen is returned to a quiet cellar called a hush, where it recovers its brightness over several weeks.
The hush beneath the Accord hall is the oldest in Solgrove. Its walls are lined with sablecore shell, a material that dampens stray resonance so that resting lumens are not disturbed.

An apprentice lumenwright is called a glimmer. A glimmer who passes the trial of first-light becomes a journeyman, called a steady, and a steady who raises a wardlumen unaided may petition to become a master, called a keeper.
The trial of first-light asks a glimmer to brighten a fresh sablecore to a stable glow within a single day, using only first-light dawnglass and a single caril fork. Few pass on their first attempt.
Keepers wear a band of woven dawnglass thread at the wrist. The number of strands marks how many wardlumens they have raised, and a keeper with seven strands is permitted to teach within the hush.

The opposite of resonance is discord. When two lumens with clashing keynotes are kept too close, they fall into discord, and both may gutter. Lumenwrights therefore space their crystals by keynote, never by size.
A keynote chart, called a concordance, maps which lumens may safely share a room. Every Accord hall keeps a great concordance painted on its ceiling, updated whenever a new keynote is discovered.
The act of moving a glowing lumen is delicate, for travel jostles its resonance. Lumens are carried in padded cases called cradles, and a courier who carries lumens is called a cradler.
Cradlers follow quiet routes through Solgrove called the soft roads, paved with sablecore gravel that muffles the rumble of cartwheels and keeps the lumens in accord during transport.

Once a year, on the night called the Kindling, every keeper brings their brightest lumen to the central plaza. Together the crystals are tuned to a single keynote, and for one hour the whole city glows as one.

The Kindling commemorates the end of the Dimming. Legend holds that a lone glimmer named Veyra rekindled the first guttered crystal by humming its keynote through the long dark, and from that single glow the city was relit.
Veyra is honored as the first keeper. Her caril fork, called the truefork, is kept in a glass cradle in the Accord hall and is struck only once each year, at the moment the Kindling begins.

Some lumenwrights specialize in the rare art of hueshaping, coaxing a lumen to glow in colors beyond the usual warm gold. A hueshaper can raise a crystal of deep azure or forest green, though such lumens burn fewer candlemarks.

Hueshaping is achieved by feeding a sablecore tinted dawnglass during its first month. Crushed riverstone yields blue, while powdered verdance leaf yields green. The technique is taught only to keepers of the inner hush.

A lumen that flickers without settling is said to be fretting. Fretting often means the crystal was tuned too quickly, and the remedy is to return it to the hush and let it rest before tuning again, more gently.
The slow patience of the craft gives rise to a Solgrove proverb: a hurried tuning makes a guttered crystal. Glimmers hear this on their first day and repeat it for the rest of their lives.

Lumenwrights keep detailed journals called tuning ledgers, recording each crystal keynote, its grade, and every session of resonance-tuning. A keeper inherits the ledgers of the lumens entrusted to them.

The price of dawnglass rises sharply in winter, when storms close the cliff paths east of the city. Wise keepers lay in a stock of first-light grade before the first frost, a practice called banking the light.
A guttered crystal that cannot be rekindled is not discarded. It is ground back into sablecore shell and used to line new hushes, so that even a spent lumen continues to protect the living ones.
Children in Solgrove play a game called catch-the-keynote, in which one child hums a pitch and the others race to match it. The game is said to train the ear of future glimmers.

The Accord recognizes four cardinal keynotes, named after the seasons. Spring lumens glow palest, summer brightest, autumn warmest, and winter steadiest. Most crystals fall between these, and their keynotes are named in fractions of the seasons.
A crystal tuned exactly to a cardinal keynote is called a true-season lumen and fetches a great many candlemarks, for its resonance is the easiest to maintain and the least prone to discord.
When a keeper dies, their entrusted lumens are gathered in the hush and held in a long rest called the mourning quiet. Only after a season may they be re-entrusted to another keeper.

The mourning quiet exists because a lumen, long tended by one hand, learns that hand. A new keeper must spend weeks tuning before the crystal accepts them, a slow courtship the guild calls earning the glow.
Lumenwrights distrust loud places. Markets, smithies, and drumhalls are kept far from any hush, for sustained noise can knock a resting lumen into fretting and undo weeks of recovery.

The quietest district of Solgrove is the Stillward, where the great hushes are clustered. Its streets are unpaved with sablecore gravel and its bells are wrapped in felt, so that no stray clang reaches the resting crystals.

A rare condition called bright-fever can strike a young lumen, in which it glows fiercely and burns through its candlemarks in days. The only cure is immediate rest in the deepest hush, where the fever may yet pass.
Bright-fever is most common in sablecores fed too much first-light dawnglass too soon. For this reason the Accord teaches a measured feeding called the slow ration, never more than a pinch each dawn.

The tools of a lumenwright are few but cherished: a set of caril forks, a feeding spoon of polished horn, a tuning ledger, and a cradle. A keeper may use the same forks for fifty years, retuning them as they wear.

Caril forks are forged from a quiet alloy called stillbronze, which holds its pitch without ringing on. A fork that begins to ring true after it is struck is said to be singing, and must be retired before it spoils a tuning.
Solgrove exports its finest hearthlumens to distant cities, but never its dawnglass, and never a beaconlumen. The Accord holds that to sell the means of the craft would be to gutter the craft itself.

Travelers often mistake a lumen for a simple lamp, but a lamp burns fuel while a lumen burns nothing. A lumen merely shares the light it has gathered through patient resonance, then rests to gather more.

The deepest secret of the craft, known only to seven-strand keepers, is how to read a sablecore before it is fed, telling from its weight and grain whether it will rise to a hearth, a ward, or a beacon.
This reading is called grain-sight, and it cannot be taught from a ledger. A keeper learns it only by handling thousands of sablecores beside a master, until the knowledge settles into the hands.
A famous saying of the keepers holds that the crystal teaches the lumenwright, not the other way around. To raise a lumen is to listen long enough that the crystal tells you what it needs.

On the morning after the Kindling, the lumens are gently detuned from the shared keynote and returned to their own. This delicate unwinding is called the parting, and a botched parting can gutter even a beaconlumen.

The youngest keeper in living memory was a glimmer named Tolen, who raised a wardlumen at nineteen by an unorthodox method of feeding at dusk rather than dawn. The Accord debated his methods for years before adopting them.

Dusk-feeding, once heresy, is now taught alongside the slow ration. The change is cited within the Accord as proof that even the oldest craft must keep listening, lest its own traditions fall into discord.

A lumen kept perfectly in accord for a hundred years is called an elder, and only a handful exist in Solgrove. Elders glow without ever needing to rest, and the keepers say they have learned the city itself as their keynote.

To stand beneath an elder lumen at midnight, when the Stillward is silent, is considered the closest thing Solgrove has to a sacred moment. Glimmers are brought there once, on the eve of their first trial, and never forget it.
The whole philosophy of lumenwrighting can be folded into a single instruction the keepers give every glimmer: feed slowly, tune gently, listen always, and the light will keep itself.
